chapter.name: Locating Places on the Earth
chapter.blurb: Maps represent an area viewed from above, using distance (scale), direction and symbols. A globe, being spherical like the Earth, is a more accurate but less portable alternative. Latitude measures distance from the Equator; longitude measures distance from the Prime Meridian; together they locate any place and relate to climate zones and time zones, including Indian Standard Time and the International Date Line.

scope_in.item: A map is a representation/drawing of an area viewed from above; an atlas is a book of maps; types of maps: physical (natural features), political (boundaries/cities), thematic (specific information); three map components: distance (scale, e.g. 1 cm = 500 m), direction (cardinal: N/E/S/W; intermediate: NE/SE/SW/NW), and symbols (standardised in India by the Survey of India)

The Earth is nearly a sphere (slightly flattened at the poles); a globe is a sphere with a map drawn on it, generally made of metal, plastic or cardboard; a sphere's surface cannot be perfectly flattened without distortion (the orange-peel idea)

Coordinates locate a place precisely, illustrated by a market-stall/chessboard analogy; latitude measures distance from the Equator (0 degrees) towards a pole (90 degrees N or S); parallels of latitude are east-west circles that shrink towards the poles; latitude broadly relates to climate: torrid (hot, near Equator), temperate (moderate), frigid (cold, near poles)

Longitude measures distance from the Prime Meridian (0 degrees, at Greenwich, agreed internationally in 1884) along the Equator, in degrees East or West up to 180 (where 180E and 180W coincide); meridians of longitude are pole-to-pole half-circles; the Prime Meridian divides Earth into Western/Eastern Hemispheres, the Equator into Northern/Southern Hemispheres; India's own historical prime meridian, the Ujjayini/madhya rekha meridian through Ujjain (about 75.8 degrees E), used by ancient astronomers such as Varahamihira; India's latitude/longitude range (about 8N-37N, 68E-97E)

The Earth rotates 360 degrees in 24 hours, i.e. 15 degrees per hour; local time increases going east from the Prime Meridian and decreases going west, by one hour per 15 degrees; standard time is one time adopted by a whole country based on a chosen meridian, rather than using every local time; Indian Standard Time (IST) is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean Time (GMT)

Time zones broadly follow 15-degree longitude bands but bend to follow international borders; very large countries can have multiple time zones (USA: 6, Russia: 11); the International Date Line lies approximately at 180 degrees longitude (opposite the Prime Meridian) and deviates from a straight line to avoid splitting countries; crossing it eastward subtracts a day, crossing it westward adds a day

concepts.name: Maps: definition, types and components
concepts.description: A map represents an area from above using scale, direction and symbols; physical, political and thematic maps serve different purposes.
concepts.idea: A map is a representation or drawing of an area viewed from above; its three main components are distance (scale), direction and symbols.
concepts.rule: Physical maps show natural features, political maps show boundaries/cities, thematic maps show specific information; a map's scale lets you calculate real-world distances from map measurements.
concepts.example: On a map with scale 1 cm = 500 m, a 3 cm distance on the map represents 1500 m in reality; the four cardinal directions plus four intermediate directions are shown using an arrow marked N.

questions.q: A friend says, 'A map with a very small scale number, like 1 cm = 10 m, is always better than a map with a large scale number, like 1 cm = 500 km, because it shows more detail.' Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: This is only partly true. A scale like 1 cm = 10 m shows much more fine detail, but it would only be practical for a very small area, like a playground; to show a whole country like India at that scale, the map would need to be impossibly large. A scale like 1 cm = 500 km suits a large area, even though it shows less fine detail. Neither scale is universally better -- it depends on the area's size and the map's purpose.
s: States the claim needs qualification, not a flat yes

concepts.name: The globe and representing the spherical Earth
concepts.description: A globe, being spherical like the Earth, represents its geography more accurately than a flat map, which inevitably distorts a sphere's surface.
concepts.idea: The Earth is nearly a sphere, slightly flattened at the poles; a globe is a sphere with a map drawn on it, representing Earth's geography more accurately than a flat map.
concepts.rule: A sphere's surface cannot be flattened onto paper without tearing or distortion, like peeling and flattening orange skin, which is why globes and flat maps each suit different purposes.
concepts.example: Peeling an orange and trying to flatten the skin without tearing demonstrates why a perfectly accurate flat map of the whole spherical Earth is not possible.

concepts.name: Latitude: parallels, the Equator, and climate zones
concepts.description: Latitude measures distance in degrees from the Equator towards a pole, relating broadly to torrid, temperate and frigid climate zones.
concepts.idea: Latitude measures the distance, in degrees, of a place from the Equator, measured along the direction toward a pole.

concepts.example: India's latitudes extend approximately from 8N to 37N; Delhi's latitude is about 29N.

concepts.name: Time zones: local time, the longitude-time relationship, and Indian Standard Time
concepts.description: The Earth's rotation (15 degrees per hour) creates differing local times by longitude; countries use one standard time for convenience, and IST is GMT+5:30.
concepts.idea: As the Earth rotates once every 24 hours (360 degrees), it turns 15 degrees every hour, so local time changes by one hour for every 15 degrees of longitude.
concepts.rule: Moving east of the Prime Meridian, local time is ahead by one hour per 15 degrees; moving west, it is behind; countries adopt one standard time rather than every local time; IST is GMT+5:30.
concepts.example: At noon GMT, local time is 1 pm at 15E and 11 am at 15W; friends in Porbandar and Tinsukia share IST but experience different actual daylight due to differing true local time.

concepts.name: Standard time across countries and the International Date Line
concepts.description: Countries organise time zones roughly by 15-degree bands adjusted to borders; the International Date Line, near 180 degrees, is where the calendar date changes.
concepts.idea: Countries organise standard times into time zones based on 15-degree longitude bands adjusted to follow borders; the International Date Line, at approximately 180 degrees, is where the date changes.
concepts.rule: Crossing the Date Line eastward subtracts a day; crossing it westward adds a day; the line bends from a straight 180-degree path to avoid splitting countries across two dates.
